definition: Random indexing is a dimensionality reduction method and computational framework for distributional semantics, based on the insight that very-high-dimensional vector space model implementations are impractical, that models need not grow in dimensionality when new items (e.g.
details: new terminology) are encountered, and that a high-dimensional model can be projected into a space of lower dimensionality without compromising L2 distance metrics if the resulting dimensions are chosen appropriately. This is the original point of the random projection approach to dimension reduction first formulated as the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, and locality-sensitive hashing has some of the same starting points. Random indexing, as used in representation of language, originates from the work of Pentti Kanerva on sparse distributed memory, and can be described as an incremental formulation of a random projection. It can be also verified that random indexing is a random projection technique for the construction of Euclidean spaces—i.e. L2 normed vector spaces. In Euclidean spaces, random projections are elucidated using the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma. The TopSig technique extends the random indexing model to produce bit vectors for comparison with the Hamming distance similarity function. explainer.lead: Random indexing is a dimensionality reduction method and computational framework for distributional semantics. It matters because it builds usable high-dimensional semantic models when full vector space implementations are impractical.

tiers.eli5: Instead of recording every word's relationship in an enormous table, you give each word a short random fingerprint; similar words end up with similar fingerprints and you never need the giant table.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it so models need not grow in dimensionality when new items such as new terminology appear, projecting a high-dimensional model into lower dimensionality. A pitfall is that L2 distances are only preserved if the resulting dimensions are chosen appropriately.
tiers.paperLevel: Based on the insight that very-high-dimensional vector space models are impractical, models need not grow in dimensionality for new items, and a high-dimensional model can be projected to lower dimensionality without compromising L2 distance metrics if dimensions are chosen appropriately; this is the random projection approach of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, with shared starting points in locality-sensitive hashing.

explainer.example: When new terminology arrives, its random index vector is simply added without resizing the model; distances between word vectors remain meaningful under suitable dimensionality.
